/Issued 1247 PM MDT Thu Aug 13 2026/ 

 - Meteorological Overview:

A southwesterly flow aloft will more or less persist across the 
Northern Rockies through the weekend into early next week. This flow 
is initially more cyclonic in nature, which will foster plenty of 
showers and thunderstorms through Friday evening across the region. 
Persistent surface winds from the east and northeast will continue 
to usher in cooler temperatures. Precipitable water values will tick 
a touch higher today, resulting in increased precipitation 
efficiency with showers and thunderstorms that develop. The most 
robust thunderstorms that develop over the next few days will be 
capable of producing at least briefly heavy rainfall. Should one of 
these stronger storms move over urban areas or burn scars, some 
localized flash flooding cannot be ruled out. Lightning and gusty 
winds will also be a concern with stronger thunderstorms. 

Heading into the weekend the nature of the southwesterly flow aloft 
becomes a bit more anti-cyclonic. That said, moisture working in 
from the southwest will combine with temperatures trending closer to 
normal to result in scattered afternoon showers and thunderstorms. 

Greater uncertainty in the pattern develops toward the middle of 
next week. At this point the main takeaway will be for scattered 
showers and thunderstorms most days with temperatures near average. 
-AM

 - Forecast Confidence & Scenarios:

Heavy Rainfall through Saturday morning...

Hi-Res Ensemble Forecast (HREF) guidance remains, and has remarkably 
been so for the past several days, consistent with showers and 
thunderstorms developing each day across the Northern Rockies as 
monsoon moisture streams northeast and over low level north-to-east 
flow in place across Southwest through North Central Montana. This 
mornings 12z RAOB from Great Falls measured PWATs at 0.97", which 
was accurately prog'd in the NAEFS since Tuesday. This consistent 
run-to-run model guidance gives increased confidence in rainfall 
amounts and locations through the end of the work week, with the 
heaviest precipitation expected to fall along and south of the 
Montana Hwy 200 over this timeframe, most notably between the 
I-90 and US Hwy 12 corridors.

Included below are tables listing 24 hour rainfall probabilities

North Central, Central, and Southwest Montana. The first table 
reflects the 24 hour period from 12PM Thursday through 12PM

Friday through 12PM Saturday.

Risk for strong thunderstorms:

While inverted-V soundings will be around across SW MT the next two 
days, these inverted-Vs are rather shallow all things considered. 
This will help reduce the risk for a strong to severe gust. At this 
time the main concern will continue to be lightning, aside from 
briefly heavy rainfall. -AM
